In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the damage by moose is spatially autocorrelated on the stand scale.
thinning of damaged trees may reduce the damage on the stand, but that the effect is likely to be small.

thinning of young pine stands may reduce the damage caused by moose if the thinned stands are left with a high density of stems and the thinning is performed in a manner that does not create gaps within the stands.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the forest industry may be able to reduce the economic losses from moose browsing and damage by using selective thinning, but the actions have to consider the spatial distribution and the interactions of browsing and damage at different scales.

the forest industry should not be too eager to remove the damaged trees in young pine forests as this may create gaps in the forest stand, increase the browsing pressure on undamaged trees and possibly reduce the growth of the remaining pines.
the forest industry may be able to reduce the economic losses due to moose damage in pine stands by performing selective thinning.
The main takeaway from our work is that
there is a strong spatial autocorrelation in browsing and damage on pine stems within young forest stands.
the spatial scale at which the thinning is carried out is crucial for the outcome of the action.
the effects of moose browsing and damage on young pine stands are spatially structured and that this structure has to be accounted for in any management actions.
